titulo: Town, places and directions: Places in town and where they are

aula.objetivo: Name places in town, say where they are with «vicino a», «davanti a» and similar expressions, ask for and give directions with the formal imperative, and choose a means of transport. Avoid the English-speaker traps: leaving out «a» after «vicino», using one imperative for everyone, and «by bus» with «per».

sessao.titulo: Places in town and where they are

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: to ask where something is, use «Dov'è…?» (where is) for one thing and «Dove sono…?» for several: «Dov'è la stazione?». STEP 2: the answer uses «essere» or «trovarsi»: «La banca è vicino alla posta». STEP 3: Italian place words usually carry a small preposition after them: «vicino a» (near), «lontano da» (far from), «davanti a» (in front of), «dietro a» (behind), «accanto a» (next to), «di fronte a» (opposite), «in fondo a» (at the end of). English says «near the station» with nothing between, but standard Italian needs the «a»: «vicino alla stazione». STEP 4: when an article follows, the preposition merges with it (lesson 10): «vicino alla posta», «davanti al museo». STEP 5: «in centro» (in the town center) has no article. «Il centro» means «the center»: «Vado in centro». STEP 6: watch the false friend «la posta»: it is the post office and also the mail, not «the post». Most of the other words look like their English cousins («ospedale», «farmacia», «museo»), and «la piazza» is the open square at the heart of a town. STEP 7: «vicino» also works as an adverb, with no object: «C'è una farmacia vicino» (There is a pharmacy nearby).
blocos.comparacao: English «near the post office» has no word between «near» and «the»; Italian «vicino alla posta» needs the preposition «a», merged with the article. The most common mistake is to forget it («vicino la posta»): you may hear that in casual speech, but standard Italian keeps the «a». Note also the false friend «posta»: it is the post office and the mail, not the person who delivers.
